newsitem.title: USA: Inflation threat lingers despite economic slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Inflation threat lingers despite economic slowdown.

text.p: Consumer confidence roared to a 28-year high in May in another sign that inflation may reignite, but a prominent group of analysts said Tuesday that the economy will throttle down from its raging first-quarter growth rate in time to contain prices.

With U.S. unemployment at a 23-year low of 4.9 percent in April and many businesses reporting labour shortages, economists predicted the Federal Reserve will continue raising interest rates later this year to ensure modest price growth.

"Sooner or later inflation will start to pick up, given the very strong growth of the economy, but I think it won't be a lot, because the Fed will be there," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.

The Conference Board said its consumer confidence index hit 127.1 in May, up from 118.5 in April, suggesting only a shallow slowdown from the blistering 5.6 percent gross domestic product growth in the first quarter.
"Certainly, these kinds of numbers are consistent with an economy moving back toward a 4 percent growth rate" by the end of 1997, said Conference Board economist Ken Goldstein.

Many experts see GDP dipping toward 2.0 percent growth in the current quarter, reflecting a pullback from one-time economic stimulants, including a large buildup in industrial inventories and unusually mild weather in the first quarter.
The National Association of Business Economists said that its members see growth near the 2 percent level through the remainder of the year and into 1998.

But even at that level, which economists believe would begin to increase unemployment and limit inflation, the association's quarterly survey showed 84 percent of its members see at least one Fed rate hike in the next six months.
"If you want a sustainable expansion here, you've got to get a little more slack in the economy," said the association's president, Mark Dadd.

The group's members on average saw only a modest hike in the federal funds rate, banks' overnight lending rate that helps set consumer and commercial loan rates, to about 6.0 percent from 5.5 percent currently.
In addition, two-thirds of the panellists said they saw no recession until 1999 or later.
The rise in consumer confidence suggests Americans will continue spending money at a healthy pace in the months ahead, said the Conference Board's Goldstein.
"The American working consumer has finally gotten over the fear of (corporate) downsizing and has finally realised that this is a strong economy and it is not breaking up," he added.
With consumer spending comprising roughly two-thirds of GDP, any acceleration now could trigger faster inflation ahead, economists cautioned.
"I'm a little concerned inflation expectations may be starting to pick up," said Mellon Bank's Berner.
One sign of moderation came from the housing market. The National Association of Realtors said existing home sales fell 2.4 percent in April to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.06 million.

While still near record levels, the decline in sales, combined with a growing supply of homes on the market, points to stable housing prices ahead, said Paul Taylor, senior economist at America's Community Bankers, a trade association.

"Even though homes are selling well, they're coming on the market faster than they're clearing it. That's good news for consumers because it will naturally constrain housing price increases," Taylor said.
